findings.detail: The old lane was workflow_dispatch on master. Branch code was only compiled and ad-hoc signed in a secretless job, and publication ran master's reviewed scripts. The new lane triggers on any push to `dev` and calls `./.github/workflows/release-provider.yml` with `secrets: inherit` (head lines 103-106). That reusable workflow is taken from the pushed commit, so whoever can push `dev` controls the workflow, the build action and the scripts. The header comment (lines 30-35) admits `dev` has no pull_request or review rule. A malicious or compromised push could edit the workflow to exfiltrate every repository secret. These include APPLE_CERTIFICATE_P12, APPLE_APP_PASSWORD, and PROD_RELEASE_KEY/STAGING_* values, since the comment says they are all repository secrets with no environment scoping. Branch code also runs in the signing job (for example the smoke test of the signed binary). The result is Developer ID signing and notarization of unreviewed code under the same team ID that the self-updater's production designated requirement accepts (release-provider.yml lines 829-834). It also exposes the prod release key that controls the trusted-binary registry. The check that master's copy of verify-source runs lives inside the attacker-editable workflow, so it does not bind. Fix: require a pull_request/review ruleset on `dev` before enabling the trigger. Bind the signing and prod secrets to protected GitHub environments, so a dev ref cannot read them. Pass explicit DEV_* secrets instead of `secrets: inherit`. Pin the reusable workflow to master with `uses: ...@master`, or a SHA.
findings.title: Unreviewed dev-branch push now runs the pushed workflow with inherited Developer ID, notarization and release secrets

findings.detail: The new Dev-Branch Lane section says a push to the d-inference `dev` branch calls `release-provider.yml` with `secrets: inherit` and gets the same Developer ID signature as master and prod builds. Such a build satisfies the self-updater's `DarkbloomCodeSignature` production requirement and the fan-helper requirement in `scripts/install.sh`. The same section states that review is not enforced on `dev`: the only protections are required signatures and a ref-creation bypass list. A single account on that bypass list, or a compromised one, could push unreviewed code. That code would be built, signed with the production Apple team identity (`SLDQ2GJ6TL`, bundle id `io.darkbloom.provider`), notarized and registered on the dev coordinator. Previously the branch lane used ad-hoc signing and a relaxed installer requirement. The doc says only the production registration and release key keep a dev build out of production, so the Developer ID signature is no longer a barrier. The lane is added with a documented missing control (a pull_request rule on `dev`). Fix: enforce the rule or an environment approval before enabling the lane, and update the threat model to cover the dev-branch signing path.
findings.title: Dev-branch pushes get production Developer ID signing, notarization and secrets while `dev` has no review rule

findings.detail: verify_workflow_source now accepts any push to refs/heads/dev when RELEASE_ENVIRONMENT=dev. verify_source(..., "dev") only checks that the commit has a GitHub-verified signature and is an ancestor of dev's head. That proves a signature exists, not that anyone reviewed the code. The updated docs (provider-release.md ~L542-546) say review is not enforced on `dev`. They also say a dev build gets the same Developer ID signature and meets the self-updater's production designated requirement (~L296-301, ~L516-518). The reusable workflow runs with `secrets: inherit`, with Apple signing, notarization and provisioning-profile secrets in the signing job. Previously, signed output came only from reviewed master ancestry or a signed tag. A writer with push access to `dev`, or a compromised account with a verified signing key, can have arbitrary provider code or workflow changes signed and notarized under team SLDQ2GJ6TL and bundle id io.darkbloom.provider. The result is a notarized binary with the production bundle id, access group and APNs topic, which can be distributed outside the intended dev lane. Fix: before enabling this path, require a pull_request and review rule on `dev` (the doc defers this to an admin) or make the gate fail unless such a rule is present. Also restrict the dev-branch workflow's access to signing secrets, for example through a protected environment.
findings.title: Unreviewed `dev` branch pushes can now obtain production Developer ID signing and notarization

findings.detail: release-dev-branch.yml now starts on any push to `dev` and calls the local ./.github/workflows/release-provider.yml with `secrets: inherit` (head ~lines 95-106). The reusable workflow, build action and scripts all come from the pushed commit. The master-side `verify-source` gate runs inside that same pushed workflow, so a malicious commit can remove it. The docs (provider-release.md ~L542) and the file comments say `dev` has no pull_request/review rule. Only signed commits and a ref-creation bypass list are required, and a verified signature does not show review. Previously the dev-branch lane was dispatch-only, ad-hoc signed and secretless, and signed output came only from reviewed master or a signed tag. A pusher to `dev`, or a compromised signing-capable account, could exfiltrate the repo-level Apple signing, notarization and release secrets. They could also have unreviewed code signed and notarized under team SLDQ2GJ6TL and bundle id io.darkbloom.provider. That signature satisfies the self-updater's production designated requirement and weakens the binary-trust assumption. Fix: add a required-review ruleset on `dev` before enabling the trigger. Scope the Apple and release secrets to protected environments with branch restrictions. Pass explicit DEV_* secrets instead of `secrets: inherit`. Pin the reusable workflow to master (`@master` or a SHA).
findings.title: Push to unreviewed `dev` runs the pushed reusable workflow with inherited secrets and Developer ID signing/notarization

findings.detail:
The new runbook (head 503-546) makes every push to the `dev` branch start `release-dev-branch.yml`. That workflow calls the reusable `release-provider.yml` with `secrets: inherit` and no GitHub environment (head 528: "All of these are repository secrets"). The build is signed with the production Developer ID. It meets the production self-updater requirement (Apple anchor, `io.darkbloom.provider`, `SLDQ2GJ6TL`) and shares the production keychain access group. The doc admits that review is not enforced on `dev` (head 542-546). The base lane was dispatch-only on master, ad-hoc signed, and ran branch code without secrets.

Trigger: anyone who can push to `dev` changes provider code, or changes the workflow YAML that runs for that push. That YAML includes the reusable workflow if it is referenced locally. The `environment == 'prod'` guards (head 531-535) live in YAML that a dev push can edit, so they do not protect secrets. Only master's source gate script is fixed.

Impact:
- Exfiltration of `PROD_RELEASE_KEY`, `PROD_R2_*` and the Apple signing and notarization credentials.
- Unreviewed code shipped under the production team signature. It could read co-installed production keychain items, such as provider tokens.
- The binary-identity assumptions in T-013 and T-054 no longer hold.

Fix: before enabling the lane, require PR review on `dev`, or keep `dev` unsigned or ad-hoc signed. Put prod and Apple secrets behind protected GitHub environments scoped to master or tags. Pass secrets explicitly instead of `secrets: inherit`. Pin the reusable workflow to master's reviewed copy.
findings.title: Unreviewed `dev` pushes would get Developer ID signing and inherited production secrets

findings.detail: verify_workflow_source (api.py head 73-80) now accepts a push to refs/heads/dev. It requires only a GitHub-verified commit on dev ancestry and RELEASE_ENVIRONMENT=dev, then returns before any master or review check. The release doc says dev has no pull_request review rule (provider-release.md head 542-546). It also says a dev build carries the same Developer ID, team SLDQ2GJ6TL, bundle ID io.darkbloom.provider and keychain access group as production. Such a build meets the self-updater's DarkbloomCodeSignature requirement and the fan-helper requirement in install.sh (head 296-301, 393-398, 516-518). Trigger: a ruleset-bypass account, or a compromise of one, pushes a signed but unreviewed commit to dev. CI then signs and notarizes arbitrary provider code under the production identity. That binary can share the production keychain group (provider tokens A-008, SE-key use A-002), pass the root fan helper's peer check (T-044), and run as the provider for a local operator, broadening T-013. Only the production registration and release key keep it out of prod's official-build registry (A-011/A-017). The doc's precondition that dev gets a review rule before the lane runs is not enforced in code. Fix: refuse dev-branch signing until branch protection requiring review is verified, for example by checking the dev ruleset through the API. Alternatively, sign dev builds with a distinct identifier, team or profile that the production designated requirement, keychain group and fan helper reject.
findings.title: Unreviewed dev-branch source now receives the production Developer ID signature and notarization

findings.detail:
Head lines 26-28 add refs/heads/dev as a second branch whose pushes publish signed dev releases (dev_push=true; previously base lines 17-19 rejected every non-master branch). The pipeline tests state that the dev-branch lane signs with the real Developer ID and that every environment's final app meets the self-updater designated requirement (identifier io.darkbloom.provider, team SLDQ2GJ6TL). The base already applied that identity to master dev builds. The new risk is that code merged only to dev now receives it too.

Trigger: anyone who can push or merge to dev, possibly under weaker protection than master, gets a published artifact with production-equivalent Apple code identity. That code can match any check keyed only on team/identifier, such as the self-updater requirement or keychain access groups like SLDQ2GJ6TL.io.darkbloom.provider. It can also be a candidate for build qualification.

The master-run verify-source gate checks workflow source, not dev-branch provider code. Impact relates to binary integrity and code identity (T-013/T-054, A-011/A-017).

Fix:
- Require dev-branch protection equivalent to master, or a distinct signing identity or bundle identifier for dev-branch builds.
- Ensure the self-updater and qualification gates reject -dev.branch.N artifacts outside DevNet.
- Update the threat model to record this new signing source.
findings.title: Dev-branch pushes now reach Developer ID signing and publication with a production-matching code identity

findings.detail: The head tests now require the caller to run the pushed commit's own `./.github/workflows/release-provider.yml` with `secrets: inherit` (lines 126-127, 137). They also require that the reusable workflow attach no GitHub `environment:` for prod, staging or dev (line 198), so prod and staging secrets are not environment-protected. Prod and staging secrets are separated only by an expression guard inside that same file (GUARDED_SECRET, lines 41-43). That file comes from the dev commit that triggered the run. These offline tests cannot stop the triggering run from executing a modified copy. Base kept dev-branch code credential-free: lines 94-100 required no secret in the build job, and lines 87-92 required publishing from master-checked-out scripts. Base lines 60-68 also barred the Apple signing identity. Trigger: anyone who can push to `dev` commits a release-provider.yml that reads PROD_* secrets without the guard, or misuses APPLE_CERTIFICATE_P12. Impact: exposure of production release-publication keys (A-005) and of the Developer ID signing and notarization identity. An attacker could then publish or register untrusted binaries (A-011) or obtain Apple-signed, notarized builds of arbitrary dev code that carry the production team identity (T-013, T-054). Fix: scope prod and staging secrets to protected GitHub environments with branch restrictions. Pass only the needed secrets explicitly instead of `inherit`. Alternatively, require `dev` to have master-equivalent branch protection and use a distinct signing identity for dev.
findings.title: Dev-push lane hands every repository secret, including Developer ID signing material, to dev-branch workflow code
